WITH first_delivered AS (
  SELECT package_id, MIN(scanned_at) AS delivered_at
  FROM package_scans
  WHERE scan_type = 'DELIVERED'
  GROUP BY package_id
), per_order AS (
  SELECT o.order_id, o.{{group_col}} AS grp, o.promised_date,
         COUNT(p.package_id)   AS packages,
         COUNT(f.delivered_at) AS delivered_packages,
         MAX((f.delivered_at AT TIME ZONE o.dest_tz)::date) AS delivered_local_date
  FROM orders o
  LEFT JOIN packages p        ON p.order_id = o.order_id
  LEFT JOIN first_delivered f ON f.package_id = p.package_id
  GROUP BY o.order_id, o.{{group_col}}, o.promised_date
), judged AS (
  SELECT grp, promised_date, delivered_local_date,
         CASE WHEN packages = 0 OR delivered_packages < packages THEN 'undelivered'
              WHEN delivered_local_date <= promised_date        THEN 'on_time'
              ELSE 'late' END AS outcome
  FROM per_order
)
SELECT promised_date,
       grp AS {{group_col}},
       COUNT(*)                                       AS orders,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE outcome = 'on_time')    AS on_time,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE outcome = 'late')       AS late,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE outcome = 'undelivered') AS undelivered,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE outcome = 'on_time') / COUNT(*), 1) AS on_time_pct,
       MAX(delivered_local_date - promised_date) FILTER (WHERE outcome = 'late') AS max_days_late
FROM judged
GROUP BY promised_date, grp
ORDER BY promised_date, grp;

Explanation. The grain of the scorecard is the order, so scans are reduced to one delivery instant per package (the first DELIVERED scan; attempts and re-synced repeats do not count), and packages to one row per order: how many packages, how many delivered, and the latest local delivery date. LEFT JOINs from orders keep orders that have no packages yet and packages that have no delivery. Each delivery is converted to the destination's local date with AT TIME ZONE dest_tz before taking the date: on a timestamptz that yields the local wall-clock time, DST included. An order is undelivered unless every package is delivered; otherwise its last package decides on time versus late. 100.0 * forces numeric division; ROUND(numeric, 1) rounds half away from zero. max_days_late is a date difference in whole days and is NULL when the filter matches no row.

WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT s.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY package_id ORDER BY scanned_at, scan_id) AS rn
  FROM package_scans s
), bounds AS (
  SELECT package_id,
         MIN(rn) FILTER (WHERE scan_type <> 'LABEL_CREATED') AS first_rn,
         MIN(rn) FILTER (WHERE scan_type = 'DELIVERED')      AS delivered_rn
  FROM ordered
  GROUP BY package_id
), kept AS (
  SELECT o.package_id, o.rn, o.facility_id, o.scanned_at,
         b.delivered_rn IS NOT NULL AS delivered
  FROM ordered o
  JOIN bounds b ON b.package_id = o.package_id
  WHERE b.first_rn IS NOT NULL
    AND o.rn >= b.first_rn
    AND (b.delivered_rn IS NULL OR o.rn <= b.delivered_rn)
), gaps AS (
  SELECT package_id, delivered, rn, facility_id,
         scanned_at AS gap_started_at,
         COALESCE(LEAD(scanned_at) OVER (PARTITION BY package_id ORDER BY rn),
                  CASE WHEN NOT delivered THEN TIMESTAMPTZ '{{as_of}}' END) - scanned_at AS gap
  FROM kept
), longest AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (package_id) package_id, delivered, gap_started_at, facility_id, gap
  FROM gaps
  WHERE gap IS NOT NULL
  ORDER BY package_id, gap DESC, rn
)
SELECT package_id, delivered, gap_started_at, facility_id,
       ROUND(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM gap) / 3600, 2) AS gap_hours
FROM longest
WHERE gap >= INTERVAL '{{min_hours}} hours'
ORDER BY gap DESC, package_id;

Explanation. A deterministic row number per package (scanned_at, then scan_id) turns "the first carrier scan" and "the first DELIVERED scan" into two integers, and the counted scans are the rows between them. LEAD over those rows gives the end of each silence; for an undelivered package the last row has no next scan, so its silence runs to as_of, while for a delivered package the DELIVERED row's NULL gap is dropped. A package with only LABEL_CREATED has no first carrier scan and is excluded. DISTINCT ON keeps the longest silence per package, the earliest on ties (by row number). Interval comparison is exact; EXTRACT(EPOCH …) returns numeric seconds in PostgreSQL 14 and later, so the rounding is exact too.

Complexity. One sort per package for the row numbers and the LEAD (they share the order), a small aggregate and a DISTINCT ON sort: O(n log n). Incrementally, each package needs only its last counted scan, its longest silence so far and whether it has been delivered.

Dialect notes. Not executed here. Snowflake and BigQuery: no DISTINCT ON (use QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY package_id ORDER BY gap DESC, rn) = 1) and no FILTER (MIN(IFF(...)) / MIN(IF(...))); gaps as DATEDIFF('second', a, b) or TIMESTAMP_DIFF(b, a, SECOND) integers instead of intervals. Spark SQL: lead and row_number as here; unix_timestamp(b) - unix_timestamp(a). MySQL 8: window functions supported; TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, a, b); no DISTINCT ON.

Edge cases built into the data. Label-to-pickup waits longer than the threshold (must not count); a silence of exactly the threshold (reported) and one just under (not reported); Hard: return pickups days after delivery, two equal longest silences at different facilities (the earlier wins), duplicate scans at the same second; Very Hard: undelivered packages whose open silence to as_of is the longest, undelivered packages scanned recently, and packages with only a label.

Common mistakes. Including LABEL_CREATED; running LEAD over every scan (so the return pickup or the label wait becomes the longest silence); reporting the facility of the scan after the silence; ORDER BY scanned_at without the scan_id tie-break; reporting the later of two equal silences; forgetting the open silence of undelivered parcels; max - min of the whole journey instead of consecutive gaps; a strict > threshold.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Per package: last counted scan time and facility, delivered flag; a timer (or a periodic scan of a "last seen" index) fires when now - last_scan ≥ threshold. (2) Compare against the facility's own scan heartbeat: if the facility has uploaded nothing either, the parcel's silence is the facility's, not the parcel's; batch-upload delay should be measured as ingested_at - scanned_at. (3) Expected silence per leg type (from history, e.g. a high percentile per origin, destination and leg) and alert on the ratio, not a global threshold. (4) Partition by scan date, cluster by package id; restrict to packages with a scan in the last N days and not yet delivered.

WITH items AS (
  SELECT account_id, usage_date, cost_cents,
         NULLIF(LOWER(TRIM(team)), '') AS team
  FROM cur_line_items
  WHERE line_item_type = 'Usage'
), tagged AS (
  SELECT account_id, usage_date, team, SUM(cost_cents)::bigint AS direct
  FROM items
  WHERE team IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY account_id, usage_date, team
), pool AS (
  SELECT account_id, usage_date, SUM(cost_cents)::bigint AS pool
  FROM items
  WHERE team IS NULL
  GROUP BY account_id, usage_date
), shares AS (
  SELECT t.account_id, t.usage_date, t.team, t.direct,
         COALESCE(p.pool, 0) AS pool,
         SUM(t.direct) OVER (PARTITION BY t.account_id, t.usage_date)::bigint AS day_tagged
  FROM tagged t
  LEFT JOIN pool p ON p.account_id = t.account_id AND p.usage_date = t.usage_date
), floored AS (
  SELECT *, (pool * direct) / day_tagged AS base,
            (pool * direct) % day_tagged AS remainder
  FROM shares
), ranked AS (
  SELECT *,
         pool - SUM(base) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id, usage_date) AS leftover,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY account_id, usage_date ORDER BY remainder DESC, team) AS rk
  FROM floored
), allocated AS (
  SELECT account_id, team, direct,
         base + CASE WHEN rk <= leftover THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS allocated
  FROM ranked
  UNION ALL
  SELECT p.account_id, 'unallocated', 0, p.pool
  FROM pool p
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM tagged t
                    WHERE t.account_id = p.account_id AND t.usage_date = p.usage_date)
)
SELECT account_id, team,
       SUM(direct)             AS direct_cents,
       SUM(allocated)          AS allocated_cents,
       SUM(direct + allocated) AS total_cents
FROM allocated
GROUP BY account_id, team
ORDER BY account_id, team;

Explanation. Normalise first: usage lines only, tag LOWER(TRIM(…)), empty string as NULL. Then two aggregates per (account, day): tagged cost per team and the untagged pool. For each team, pool * direct / day_tagged on BIGINTs is floor division (all values are non-negative) and % the remainder. The casts matter: in PostgreSQL SUM(bigint) returns numeric, and numeric / does not truncate, so without ::bigint every share silently becomes a fraction of a cent. The pool minus the sum of the floors is the number of leftover cents (always less than the number of teams); ROW_NUMBER() over (remainder DESC, team) hands them out one each, so every pool is allocated exactly. A pool with no tagged usage that day has nobody to follow and is reported as 'unallocated' (the UNION ALL branch). Finally add each team's days up. Integers throughout: no floating point ever touches money.

Complexity. Two aggregates over the line items, a join on (account, day) and two window sorts over (teams × days): linear in the line items plus O(k log k) per pool. At scale, materialise the daily (account, day, team) tagged cost and the daily pool; the allocation runs on that small table.

Dialect notes. Not executed here. Integer division differs: BigQuery / returns FLOAT64 (use DIV(pool * direct, day_tagged) and MOD); Snowflake / returns a decimal (use FLOOR(pool * direct / day_tagged) or TRUNC, and MOD); Spark SQL / returns double (use div and %); MySQL uses DIV and MOD. ROW_NUMBER() and window sums are the same everywhere. NULLIF(LOWER(TRIM(team)), '') is portable.

Edge cases built into the data. Pools that leave one or more cents over (all levels); Hard: several days per account (daily pools differ from a monthly split), a pool with three equal teams and one or two leftover cents (the tie-break decides), credit and tax lines; Very Hard: tag values with stray spaces and capitals, empty-string tags (untagged), and a day on which an account has only untagged usage ('unallocated').

Common mistakes. Forgetting that SUM(bigint) is numeric in PostgreSQL, so / stops being floor division; ROUND(pool * direct / tagged) per team (does not sum to the pool); floating-point division; dropping the leftover cents; RANK() (ties share a rank and both get a cent, over-allocating); splitting the whole period at once; including credits or tax; comparing raw tag strings; losing pools with no tagged usage; forgetting that the pool's own account bounds its teams.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Late line items (and restated ones) change a past day's pool or weights; keep the allocation per day and per report version, recompute changed days only, and publish month-close numbers from a frozen version. (2) Drivers such as bytes transferred, request counts or vCPU-hours need usage metrics joined at the same grain; a strong answer names the data each needs and the gaming risk. (3) Daily (account, day, team) tagged cost and (account, day) pool tables, partitioned by day; the allocation is a small job over those. (4) Allocate in stages over a DAG (shared → platform teams → product teams); a cycle means the stage order is undefined, so the model must forbid it or solve it as a linear system.

Rubric anchors. 2: proportional split with rounding errors (totals do not match the pool). 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains why largest remainder is fair and how to make the allocation reproducible after late data.

from collections import defaultdict

def on_demand_unit_seconds(usages, commitments):
    deltas = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(int))   # family -> time -> change in (used - committed)
    result = {}
    for start, end, family, units in usages:
        result[family] = 0
        if end > start:
            deltas[family][start] += units
            deltas[family][end] -= units
    for start, end, family, units in commitments:
        if family in result and end > start:
            deltas[family][start] -= units
            deltas[family][end] += units
    for family, changes in deltas.items():
        level, prev, total = 0, None, 0     # level = used(t) - committed(t) on the current stretch
        for t in sorted(changes):
            if prev is not None and level > 0:
                total += level * (t - prev)
            level += changes[t]
            prev = t
        result[family] = total
    return result

Explanation. On-demand usage is the positive part of used − committed, and that difference only changes at interval endpoints. Each usage contributes +units at its start and −units at its end; a commitment the opposite. Summing changes per (family, time) applies every change at a time at once, so the order of a stop and a start at the same second is irrelevant and half-open intervals come out right. Walking the sorted times, the difference is constant between consecutive times; its positive part times the gap is that stretch's on-demand amount. Families are independent; families with only commitments never enter result; a zero-length usage enters result with no change.

Complexity. O((n + c) log(n + c)) for the sort, O(n + c) memory. A per-second loop is O(horizon) per family (about 126 million seconds in the timing test, and an array that large); rescanning every usage for every elementary interval is O(n²).

Common mistakes. Closed intervals (a back-to-back pair counted as overlapping for one second); clamping per interval instead of per moment (max(0, units − commitment) for each usage separately); allowing negative contributions (banking spare commitment); processing a start before a stop at the same second and integrating in between; dropping zero-length usages' families; reporting commitment-only families; mixing families in one sweep.

Follow-up guidance. (1) The sweep yields, for each value of used, the total time it held; cost(C) = commitment price × C × period + on-demand price × Σ time × max(0, used − C). It is convex in C, so evaluate it at the distinct used levels (or ternary search). (2) Partition by family (and time bucket); each worker emits per-bucket change events; one reducer per family sorts and sweeps, with intervals split at bucket boundaries. (3) Normalise usage into the commitment's units with a ratio per family; the state becomes one shared pool consumed by several families, which needs an allocation order. (4) SQL can produce the change events and even the running sum (SUM(delta) OVER (ORDER BY t)) and the integral with LEAD(t); what it cannot do cheaply is anything that depends on the order of allocation across families.

Rubric anchors. 2: correct on samples but per-second or quadratic, or a boundary error. 3: correct and O(n log n) with all same-time changes applied before integrating. 4: also derives the optimal commitment level from the sweep.

Strong signals. Asks whether intervals are half-open and whether spare commitment carries over before coding. Red flags. A per-second array without noticing the horizon; claiming the answer is total usage − total commitment.

import heapq

def assign_doors(trailers, doors):
    arrivals = sorted(trailers)                  # by arrival minute; the yard heap decides ties
    free = list(range(1, doors + 1))             # heap of free door numbers (already a heap)
    busy = []                                    # heap of (end_min, door)
    yard = []                                    # heap of (priority, arrival_min, trailer_id, unload_min)
    out = {}
    i, n, now = 0, len(arrivals), None
    while i < n or yard:
        if not yard:
            now = arrivals[i][0] if now is None else max(now, arrivals[i][0])
        elif not free:
            now = busy[0][0]
        while busy and busy[0][0] <= now:
            heapq.heappush(free, heapq.heappop(busy)[1])
        while i < n and arrivals[i][0] <= now:
            arrival, tid, unload, prio = arrivals[i]
            heapq.heappush(yard, (prio, arrival, tid, unload))
            i += 1
        while free and yard:
            _, _, tid, unload = heapq.heappop(yard)
            door = heapq.heappop(free)
            out[tid] = (door, now)
            heapq.heappush(busy, (now + unload, door))
    return out

Explanation. Time jumps between the only moments that matter. After every assignment round, either no door is free or the yard is empty. If the yard is empty, the next decision is at the next arrival; if it is not, the next decision is when the next door frees up (arrivals before then simply join the yard). At each moment the code first frees every door whose unload has ended (so a door freed at t is usable at t), then admits every trailer that has arrived by t (so an urgent trailer arriving at t competes), then assigns while a door and a trailer are both available: the yard heap gives the first trailer by (priority, arrival, trailer_id) and the free-door heap gives the lowest door number. Trailer ids are unique, so heap tuples never compare the unload field.

Complexity. Each trailer is pushed and popped once from the yard, and each assignment pushes and pops one door from each door heap: O(n log n + n log d), O(n + d) memory. Scanning the yard for the next trailer is O(yard) per assignment; the timing test's yard reaches tens of thousands of trailers. Scanning all doors per assignment is O(d) each.

Common mistakes. Freeing doors after admitting or assigning (a door freed at t sits idle until the next event); admitting only the trailers that arrived strictly before t; first-come-first-served ignoring priority, or priority without the arrival tie-break; taking any free door instead of the lowest number; relying on the input being sorted; stepping minute by minute; preempting an unload in progress.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Record start − arrival per trailer; the mean is a running sum; an exact 95th percentile needs the waits (or a sort per priority at the end), and a streaming answer accepts an approximate quantile sketch with a stated error. (2) One free-door heap per door type; a trailer that fits several types takes the earliest/lowest across the heaps it fits. (3) Aging: effective priority improves with waiting time; in a heap that means either periodic re-keying or a key such as arrival + weight × priority that does not change over time. (4) Sites are independent: one task per site (embarrassingly parallel), store per-trailer assignments partitioned by site and season for analysis.

Rubric anchors. 2: right outputs on samples but stepping minutes or scanning the yard. 3: correct and O(n log n) with all three heaps. 4: also a sound answer on door types or aging.

Strong signals. Asks what happens when a door frees and a trailer arrives at the same minute, and whether urgent trailers preempt. Red flags. A single sorted list re-sorted after every arrival; "just add more doors" when asked about starvation.

import heapq
from bisect import bisect_left

DAY = 1440


def earliest_arrival(lanes, handling, origin, dest, ready, daily=False):
    out = {}
    for u, v, deps in lanes:
        if not deps:
            continue
        deps = sorted(deps)
        times = [d for d, _ in deps]
        best_from = [0] * len(deps)          # earliest arrival using departure i or later
        m = None
        for i in range(len(deps) - 1, -1, -1):
            a = deps[i][0] + deps[i][1]
            if m is None or a < m:
                m = a
            best_from[i] = m
        out.setdefault(u, []).append((v, times, best_from))

    arrive = {origin: ready}
    heap = [(ready, origin)]
    while heap:
        t, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if t > arrive[u]:
            continue                          # a stale heap entry
        if u == dest:
            return t
        leave = t if u == origin else t + handling.get(u, 0)
        for v, times, best_from in out.get(u, ()):
            if daily:
                day, minute = divmod(leave, DAY)
                i = bisect_left(times, minute)
                at = (day + 1) * DAY + best_from[0]          # any departure tomorrow
                if i < len(times):
                    at = min(at, day * DAY + best_from[i])  # a later one today
            else:
                i = bisect_left(times, leave)
                if i == len(times):
                    continue
                at = best_from[i]
            if at < arrive.get(v, at + 1):
                arrive[v] = at
                heapq.heappush(heap, (at, v))
    return None

Explanation. Waiting is allowed, so for every lane the arrival as a function of the ready minute is non-decreasing. If you are ready later, the set of catchable departures can only shrink. Handling adds a constant, so it keeps the property. This "FIFO" property is what lets Dijkstra settle each node at its earliest arrival. Per lane, departures are sorted by minute, and best_from[i] holds the earliest arrival using departure i or any later one. One binary search then gives the best catchable departure. The best one need not be the next one: an express may leave later and arrive earlier. Handling is added when leaving an intermediate node, never at the origin, and the search stops when the destination is popped, so no handling is added there. With daily schedules, the earliest arrival is the better of a remaining departure today (day·1440 + best_from[i]) and any departure tomorrow ((day+1)·1440 + best_from[0]). A departure two or more days later is the same departure, later. Transits longer than a day need no special case, because arrival minutes are absolute.

Complexity. Sorting all departures costs O(D log D). Dijkstra costs O(L log N) heap work plus one binary search per lane relaxation. The timing test (3 000 nodes, 20 000 lanes, 200 000 departures) runs in about 0.15 s in CPython. Relaxing every lane until nothing changes needs about one pass per hop of the 3 000-hop main route. That is billions of departure checks, and it takes minutes.

Dialect notes. In Java or C++ use a priority queue of (arrival, node) with lazy deletion, as here, and Collections.binarySearch or lower_bound on the sorted minutes. Minutes fit easily in 32-bit integers over months. In a SQL engine, earliest arrival is a recursive CTE with a MIN per node. It is correct only if every node's minimum is propagated, and engines that do not support aggregation in the recursive step make this awkward. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Origin equals destination; no lane reaches the destination; every departure already gone; a departure exactly at the ready minute; one a minute before; handling that misses a tight connection; handling defined at the origin and destination but not applied; (Hard) a later express that arrives earlier, a two-hop route beating the direct lane, and waiting for a faster later departure; (Very Hard, daily) ready after the last departure of the day, tomorrow's express beating tonight's slow truck, ready on day 3 with a transit longer than a day, and a departure exactly at the ready minute on a later day.

Common mistakes. Taking the next departure instead of the best catchable one; adding handling at the origin or destination; > instead of >= for catching a departure; BFS by hop count; a visited set that marks a node when it is first reached instead of when it is popped; for daily schedules, using % 1440 on the arrival and losing the day, or considering only today's departures.

Follow-up guidance. (1) With capacity the FIFO property breaks for an individual package, because a full truck can make "earlier" worse. Promises need either reserved capacity per package, which is a booking system, or a buffer. Recompute as trucks fill. (2) Use distributions or percentiles per lane from historical scans. A 95% promise is not the sum of per-lane 95th percentiles, so simulate or convolve, and track whether promises are actually met. (3) Precompute a profile (earliest arrival as a function of ready time) per origin and destination region with a profile search such as connection scan, and refresh it on schedule changes. (4) Index packages by the planned departure they ride. On a cancellation, recompute only those packages and the ones behind them, and alert when a promise moves.

Strong signals. Asks whether the package can wait, and whether departures on one lane all take the same time. Red flags. "Dijkstra always works on graphs" with no mention of the property; ignoring transits that cross midnight.

def _stock(stock, fc, sku):
    return stock.setdefault((fc, sku), {"on_hand": 0, "reserved": 0})


def process_inventory(events):
    stock = {}          # (fc, sku) -> counters
    lines = {}          # (order, sku) -> reservation
    rejected = []
    for ev in events:
        t = ev["type"]
        if t in ("receive", "adjust"):
            _stock(stock, ev["fc"], ev["sku"])["on_hand"] += ev["qty"]
        elif t == "reserve":
            s = _stock(stock, ev["fc"], ev["sku"])
            if ev["qty"] <= s["on_hand"] - s["reserved"]:            # the last unit can be sold
                s["reserved"] += ev["qty"]
                lines[(ev["order"], ev["sku"])] = {"fc": ev["fc"], "sku": ev["sku"],
                                                   "qty": ev["qty"], "state": "reserved"}
            else:
                rejected.append([ev["order"], ev["sku"]])
        elif t == "cancel":
            line = lines.get((ev["order"], ev["sku"]))
            if line and line["state"] == "reserved":                  # only a live reservation
                _stock(stock, line["fc"], line["sku"])["reserved"] -= line["qty"]
                line["state"] = "cancelled"
        elif t == "ship":
            line = lines.get((ev["order"], ev["sku"]))
            if line and line["state"] == "reserved":
                s = _stock(stock, line["fc"], line["sku"])
                s["on_hand"] -= line["qty"]
                s["reserved"] -= line["qty"]                           # the reservation is consumed
                line["state"] = "shipped"
    return {
        "stock": {
            fc + "/" + sku: {
                "on_hand": s["on_hand"],
                "reserved": s["reserved"],
                "available": s["on_hand"] - s["reserved"],           # may be negative
            }
            for (fc, sku), s in stock.items()
        },
        "rejected": rejected,
    }

The planted bugs, their symptoms and their fixes.

  1. Ship does not release the reservation. on_hand drops but reserved stays, so every shipped line is counted against availability for ever. Symptom: units "reserved" for orders that shipped weeks ago, and availability far below the shelf count. Fix: reserved -= qty on ship.
  2. Strict comparison at the boundary. qty < available refuses an order for exactly the units left. Symptom: the last unit of an item is never sold. Fix: <=.
  3. Availability clamped at zero. max(0, on_hand - reserved) hides an oversold centre after a negative adjustment. Symptom: the dashboard says 0 where operations needs to see −1 and re-source an order. Fix: report the signed value.
  4. Lines keyed by order id only. A multi-line order's second line overwrites the first in lines, so a cancel or ship for one SKU acts on the other line's record. Symptom: cancelling one line releases the other line's units, and the cancelled line stays reserved. Fix: key lines by (order, sku).
  5. Cancel without a state check. A second cancel, or a cancel after shipping, releases the units again, so reserved can go negative and availability creeps up. Symptom: availability drifts upward after double cancels. Fix: release only when the line is reserved.

Each bug has its own check: shipping, an exact-boundary reservation, a negative adjustment, a two-line order with one cancel, and a double cancel. The cancel-after-ship check passes on the original code by accident, because bugs 1 and 5 cancel out: the ship leaves the units reserved and the cancel releases them. It fails once bug 1 alone is fixed, and passes again when bug 5 is fixed too. Two bugs that hide each other are worth discussing with the candidate.

Explanation. Inventory reservation is a small state machine per order line (reserved → shipped or cancelled; rejected lines never enter it) on top of two counters per centre and SKU. Every transition must be guarded by the line's current state and must keep available = on_hand − reserved meaningful, including when it is negative.

Complexity. O(n) time, O(lines + centre-SKU pairs) memory. The timing test is 200 000 events.

Dialect notes. In SQL the same rules are conditional updates: UPDATE stock SET reserved = reserved + :q WHERE fc = :fc AND sku = :sku AND on_hand - reserved >= :q, and UPDATE lines SET state = 'cancelled' WHERE order_id = :o AND sku = :s AND state = 'reserved' followed by the stock update only if a row changed. A clamp written as GREATEST(0, …) in a reporting view hides the oversell the same way. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Ship then report; reserve exactly the available units; one unit too many; a negative adjustment below reserved; a two-line order with one line cancelled; a double cancel; stock at another centre; a cancel and a ship for rejected or unknown lines; a cancel after shipping.

Common mistakes. Fixing the boundary but keeping the clamp because "negative stock is impossible" (it is not impossible for availability); fixing the key for reserve but not for cancel and ship; adding the state check to cancel but releasing on ship twice; rewriting the processor instead of making minimal fixes; changing the output to omit rejected lines' stock entries.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Serialise per (centre, SKU): partition the event stream by that key, or use a conditional update in the database so that the second reservation sees the first. A process-local lock is not enough across hosts. (2) Ship and cancel are already idempotent with the state check. Receive and adjust are not, so give each event an id and record applied ids in the same transaction as the counter change. (3) Expire holds with a TTL and an explicit expiry event that goes through the same state check. Expiring too early oversells when the customer completes checkout. (4) Re-source the newest or least time-critical orders to other centres first. Operations decides with a clear rule. The customer sees a revised date only if no centre can meet the promise.

AMZ-L2-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Landing. Each source lands raw and immutable in object storage, with a manifest row per file: source, business date or period, version, content hash, received time and row count. A re-sent file with the same hash is a no-op. A different file for the same day or period is a new version and is never an overwrite. Order and shipment events arrive by CDC or event export. Payment files arrive daily. Settlement reports arrive per seller and period with a version number.
  • Normalised layers. shipment_charges (shipment_id, order_id, order_line_id, amount_minor, currency, charged_at). refunds (refund_id, order_line_id, amount_minor, currency, refunded_at). settlement_rows (seller_id, period, version, order_line_id, row_type sale|fee|refund|adjustment, amount_minor, currency, settlement_currency, fx_rate). Order lines and shipments come from the marketplace with order_line_id → shipment_id mapping, and quantities split across shipments.
  • Matching grain. The order line within a shipment (order_line_id, shipment_id) is the finest grain all sources share: charges are per shipment and allocated to lines, settlements are per line, and refunds are per returned line. Results roll up to order, seller, period and currency.
  • Match states. matched; timing (one side expected later, with an expected-by date such as the next settlement after shipment, or payment within a day); amount_mismatch with a classified reason (fx, fee rounding, partial refund, unknown); missing_payment, missing_settlement, unexpected_settlement; refund_unsettled while within the refund window. Each state has an owner and an age.
  • Determinism. A run for business date D reads explicitly pinned versions of every input (recorded in a run manifest), recomputes D's partition and overwrites it atomically. A newer version triggers a rerun of affected dates and periods. Results carry run_id and input versions.
  • Currency. Match in the transaction currency first. A settlement in another currency is compared through the rate that the settlement report states, so conversion differences are explained, not broken. Rounding is per line, as the report rounds. A residual difference within a documented tolerance is classified as rounding and summed separately, never silently absorbed.
  • Outputs. Finance: a daily break summary by state, currency and age, period close status, and a change log when a closed period is re-issued. Seller support: a per-seller statement view that explains each settlement row against order lines, with version history.

Competing designs to accept. A warehouse-native SQL pipeline (dbt-style models) with snapshot tables for versions; a Spark job over a lakehouse with MERGE into a results table keyed by line; a streaming pre-match for payments with a daily batch for settlements. Any is fine if reruns are deterministic and versions are kept. Event-sourcing the match state (each state change as a row) is a strong option for audit.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Ever-growing open items rescanned every day (partition open items by expected-by date, and age them out to a manual queue); matching on order id only, which hides partial shipments; floats; latest-version-only storage, which makes old statements impossible to explain; time-zone boundaries for the business date; a reference format change breaking joins silently.

Incident guidance.

  • A closed period's settlement report is re-issued with corrected fees: land it as a new version, rerun matching for that seller, period and the affected lines, and diff the old results against the new. Post the differences into the current open period as adjustments rather than reopening a closed period, unless finance policy says otherwise. Tell seller support what changed and why.
  • Refund file arrives twice, the second copy larger: the second copy is a new version (different hash). Rows are deduplicated by refund_id, so the extra 2% are new refunds and are matched, while repeats change nothing. Rerun the day. Alert if any refund_id changes amount between versions.
  • Shipment reference format change: break counts jump by two orders of magnitude. That is a pipeline failure, not a finance problem. Detect it with a match-rate monitor per source and day, hold publication of the day's results, normalise both formats in the join (or add a mapping), and rerun. Add a data contract test on the reference format.

Follow-up guidance. (1) New version, recompute affected keys, a diff with reasons, adjustments in the open period, and history kept for the seller statement. (2) Two shipments give two charges allocated to the line. Two partial refunds match two refund rows. Settlement rows reference the line, so match at line-and-shipment grain and sum per line for refunds. (3) Use the rate stated by the settlement for conversion, and classify the residual. Never revalue history with today's rate. (4) Immutable inputs, run manifests with input versions, code version, and results by run id. (5) Index open items by expected-by date, close or escalate items past the window, and do not rescan matched history.

Rubric anchors. 2: a join on order id with appended daily results; no versioning; no timing state. 3: immutable versioned landing, line-level matching, explicit states including timing, deterministic reruns by partition overwrite. 4: also currency and rounding handled as classified differences, a re-issue process with diffs and seller-facing explanations, monitors that tell a pipeline failure from a finance break, and bounded open-item work.

Strong signals. Asks which grain each source produces before choosing a key; treats "timing" as a first-class state. Red flags. "Overwrite the old report with the new one"; tolerance thresholds that silently hide differences.

AMZ-L2-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Ingestion API. Authenticated per account. Each batch carries (account, log_group, stream, sequence) and a payload hash. The front end validates size and timestamps, applies per-account rate quotas (reject or throttle with a retry-after), and writes to the buffer before acknowledging. A deduplication store keyed by batch identity with a TTL longer than the agents' retry horizon (hours) makes retries harmless. The key is checked before the write and recorded atomically with it, or deduplicated downstream on the same key.
  • Buffer. A partitioned durable log keyed by (account, log_group, stream). Large accounts are spread across several partitions by stream, and small accounts share partitions. Per-account quotas at the API keep a single tenant from filling a shared partition. A very large account can be moved to dedicated partitions.
  • Processing. Stream processors parse known formats, extract fields (request id, status, latency), redact configured patterns, attach arrival time, and keep the line's own timestamp. Lines with timestamps far in the future or past beyond a window (for example 14 days back, 2 hours ahead) are kept but flagged, and written to the arrival-time partition with a pointer, so they are not lost.
  • Hot tier. The last hour or day of each account, in an index (inverted index on selected fields such as request id and trace id, plus time) for the interactive target. It is sized by retention of the hot window only.
  • Cold tier. Compressed columnar files in object storage, laid out as account / log_group / event_date / hour. Per-file min/max timestamps and bloom filters on request id let a scan skip files. A streaming writer produces small files every minute. Compaction merges them per hour once the hour is sealed (watermark plus a grace period) and swaps them atomically with a table format (Iceberg/Delta style) or a manifest, so readers see either the old files or the new ones.
  • Late data. Lines go to their event-time partition. A late write reopens that hour for compaction, and a sealed hour that receives late lines gets a delta file and is compacted again later. Search covers the event time asked for, so late lines are found.
  • Retention. Account first in the path makes deletion a prefix or partition drop per account and day, with no rewrite of other tenants' data. A shortened retention runs a deletion job for the newly expired range within a day, verifies by listing, and records evidence. The hot tier expires by time.
  • Isolation and billing. Account id is part of every path and query predicate, enforced by the query service, never by the client. Ingested bytes are counted at the API after deduplication and validation, from the accepted batch record, so retries do not double-bill. Malformed lines are counted and reported separately.
  • Health metrics. Buffer lag per partition and per large account, deduplication hits, rejected and throttled batches per account, files per partition and compaction backlog, late-line ratio, deletion backlog, query latency percentiles by tier.

Competing designs to accept. Index-everything search clusters for the hot tier (accept if the candidate prices it); scan-only designs with heavy partition pruning and bloom filters (accept if the latency target is met for the last hour); a managed stream plus a lakehouse table format; per-account log groups as the unit of isolation. Each has trade-offs in cost against latency.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Hot partitions from a single large account; small-file explosion; compaction racing with readers; a deduplication store that grows without bound or expires too soon; late data invisible after compaction; retention deletes that rewrite shared files; billing double-counted on retries.

Incident guidance.

  • Debug logging sends 40% of {{ingest}}: per-account quotas throttle at the API, so other tenants' latency is unaffected. Alert the customer, and offer a temporary raise that is billed. The buffer partitions of that account fall behind and the others do not. If the quota was too generous, the shared partitions show lag, so move the account to dedicated partitions.
  • Twenty minutes of batches arrive twice: batch identity is within the deduplication TTL, so the duplicates are acknowledged and dropped. Watch the deduplication hit rate spike, and confirm billed bytes did not move. If the outage exceeded the TTL, deduplicate downstream on the same key during compaction.
  • Lines two days late are missing: check where they were written. If the processor put them in the arrival-time partition, or the late window was shorter than two days, they are stored but not where search looks. Fix by writing by event time within the window, reopen and re-compact the affected hours, and backfill the misplaced lines. Document the window for customers.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Throttling at the API with retry-after; the account's lag grows; others see nothing; alert and possible re-partitioning. (2) Event-time partition plus delta files and a later compaction; the hot tier may not hold them; search uses event time. (3) Partition drops for the newly expired range, a deletion job with verification, and the hot tier purged; prove it with listings and a deletion log. (4) Count once at acceptance, after deduplication; malformed lines counted but not billed, or billed by a documented rule. (5) Bloom filters or a secondary index on request id per hour; compaction sorted by request id; extra write cost compared with scan cost saved.

Rubric anchors. 2: a single shared index or bucket with time-only partitions; no batch identity; no compaction plan. 3: batch deduplication, account-first layout, quotas, compaction with atomic swaps, retention by partition drop. 4: also late and future timestamps handled explicitly, exact billing under retries, credible per-incident responses, and a cost argument for hot versus cold.

Strong signals. Puts the account first in the layout because of retention and isolation, and says why; sizes the deduplication window from the agents' retry behaviour. Red flags. Isolation enforced by client-side filters; "just keep everything in the search index".

AMZ-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • OLTP entities.
    • orders (order_id, customer_id, marketplace, placed_at, currency): a header only, with no quantities and no status that summarises lines.
    • order_lines (order_line_id, order_id, seller_id, sku, category_id, qty_ordered, unit_price_minor, promo_alloc_minor, tax_minor, fulfilment_channel network|seller, created_at). Every line has exactly one seller (first party is a seller id).
    • line_cancellations (cancellation_id, order_line_id, qty, reason, cancelled_at).
    • shipments (shipment_id, order_id, fulfilment_centre_or_seller, carrier, shipped_at) and shipment_lines (shipment_id, order_line_id, qty, kind original|replacement). A stable shipment_line_id comes from the source system or a deterministic hash of (shipment_id, order_line_id, kind) — never from the position in a list.
    • returns (return_id, order_id, started_at, reason), return_lines (return_id, order_line_id, shipment_line_id NULL, qty, received_at NULL, disposition).
    • refunds (refund_id, order_line_id, return_id NULL, amount_minor, issued_at, reason).
    • Invariants (checked by the order service on every write and re-verified asynchronously): Σ cancelled + Σ shipped(original) + open = qty_ordered with open ≥ 0; Σ returned ≤ Σ shipped (original + replacement); Σ refunded ≤ line charge.
  • Change capture. Either an outbox of domain events (LineCancelled, LineShipped, ReturnStarted, ReturnReceived, RefundIssued) written in the same transaction as the state change, or CDC on the movement tables. Because quantity changes are rows (insert-only), CDC never loses an intermediate state; CDC on a mutable counter column could.
  • Facts.
    • fct_order_line_movement (append-only, one row per movement): line, movement type (ordered, cancelled, shipped, replacement_shipped, return_started, return_received, refunded), signed units, signed amount_minor, event time, seller, category, date keys. Net units = Σ signed units over a chosen set of movement types, so every team's definition is a filter on one table.
    • fct_order_line_snapshot (accumulating snapshot, one row per line): ordered/cancelled/shipped/returned/refunded quantities and amounts, first_shipped_at, last_return_at, is_closed. Rebuilt from movements for lines touched in the window (MERGE by partition of order date).
    • Dimensions: seller, product/category (type 2 for category re-mapping), date, fulfilment channel.
  • Definition (one acceptable wording). Net units sold for a period = units shipped (original shipments only) in orders placed in the period − units returned and received against those lines; cancellations never count as sold; replacements are neither sales nor returns of new units. Report the provisional value until the period is older than the return window plus a lag, then close it.
  • Return rate. Cohort by ship month: returned units of lines shipped in the month ÷ units shipped (original) in the month. Replacement returns are tracked separately (they are returns of a replacement, not a second sale).
  • Refunds before receipt. refunds with return_id whose return line has no received_at: an "exposure" measure for finance, aged by days since refund.
  • Access. Seller-facing marts filter by seller_id at the row level; first-party lines never reach seller views.

Competing designs to accept. An event-sourced order service where the event log is the source of truth and the OLTP tables are projections (if invariants are checked before events are accepted). Only an accumulating snapshot plus a raw event table. A single "line quantity ledger" table with a movement-type column instead of separate cancellation/shipment/return tables, if the referencing (which shipment a return came from) is kept.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Order-grain modelling that cannot represent partial states; counters overwritten on the line (history lost, CDC races); replacement shipments miscounted; shipment-line identity unstable across updates; promotions allocated at order level and re-allocated after a cancellation (restates closed months); return rates by return date mixed with sales by order date; huge MERGE cost on the snapshot at {{daily_orders}} a day (partition by order date and only touch open lines).

Incident guidance.

  • Return rate above 100% for a category: replacement shipments were not counted as shipments while their returns were. Contain by excluding replacement returns from the rate (or counting replacements in a separate denominator) and labelling the dashboard; fix the matching so a return links to the shipment line it came from; add a check that returned ≤ shipped per line and per seller-category, which would have paged.
  • Net sales no longer sum to finance after promo re-allocation: the re-allocation edited allocated amounts on lines in a closed month. Do not edit history: write the re-allocation as adjustment movements dated when they happened; restate only through a published restatement with the delta per seller; add a reconciliation of Σ seller net sales to the finance total per month that runs before statements go out.
  • Shipment lines re-numbered upstream, split lines double-counted: the key was positional. Derive a stable key (source id, or a hash of shipment id + order line id + kind), deduplicate the affected window by that key, rebuild the snapshot for lines touched, and add a contract test that a shipment line's key survives an update. The higher {{split_share}} is, the larger the blast radius: quantify it from the movement fact.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Check in the order service before commit plus an asynchronous checker; a breaking line is quarantined from seller statements and alerted, never silently clipped. (2) Original shipped 1, replacement shipped 1, returned 1 (the replacement): net sold 1, return rate for originals 0, replacement return tracked separately. (3) Re-allocation is an adjustment movement in the current period; the closed month is restated only by policy. (4) Close after {{return_window_days}} days plus processing lag; show "provisional" before. (5) Movements append-only (cheap), snapshot rebuilt for touched lines only; both is the strongest answer.

Rubric anchors. 2: an orders table with a status, or line counters overwritten, and a return rate with no cohort. 3: order-line grain, movements as rows, separate shipment/return/refund entities, a movement fact and a stated net-units definition. 4: also replacement handling, stable shipment-line identity, promotion re-allocation without editing closed months, refunds-before-receipt exposure, and a close for return rates.

Strong signals. States the line invariants before drawing tables; separates "sold" from "shipped" and "returned" from "refunded". Red flags. Order-level quantities; deleting a cancelled line; net sales computed from current line state for past months.

AMZ-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Declared.
    • inbound_plans (plan_id, seller_id, created_at) and inbound_plan_versions (plan_id, version, sku, qty, edited_at); the version in force when the shipment is marked shipped is frozen as the declaration.
    • inbound_shipments (shipment_id, plan_id, seller_id, destination_fc, carrier, marked_shipped_at, status): one per fulfilment centre after the split.
    • boxes (box_id, shipment_id, label, declared_at) and box_contents (box_id, sku, qty, version); a contents correction after shipping is a new version with evidence, and the reconciliation uses the latest accepted version.
  • Observed. receiving_events (event_id UNIQUE, fc_id, box_id NULL, shipment_id NULL, sku, unit_qty, kind box_arrived|checked_in_sellable|checked_in_damaged|unexpected_unit, occurred_at, received_by_pipeline_at). Append-only; deduplicated by event id at ingestion. Box arrival at an unplanned fulfilment centre is recorded where it physically happened and matched by box label to its shipment.
  • Resolved. discrepancy_cases (case_id, shipment_id, sku, qty, opened_at, status opened|investigating|found|reimbursed|declaration_error, resolved_at) and reimbursements (reimbursement_id, case_id, qty, amount_minor, currency, paid_at); a later find of a reimbursed unit creates a reversal of the reimbursement (or an inventory adjustment), never a delete.
  • Invariant (per shipment × SKU). declared = sellable + damaged + found + reimbursed + declaration_error + open. Open must reach 0 by the investigation window; a scheduled check lists violations.
  • Reconciled view and facts. fct_inbound_reconciliation (one row per shipment × SKU, accumulating: declared, received sellable/damaged, found, reimbursed, error, open, first_arrival_at, sellable_at, closed_at); fct_receiving_daily (fulfilment centre × seller × day aggregates of check-ins); the unit-level events are kept in cheap storage for a limited period.
  • Definitions. Received = checked in at the fulfilment centre; sellable = put away and available. Discrepancy rate = units in discrepancy cases ÷ declared units, by shipment cohort (shipped date), final once every shipment in the cohort is closed or older than {{receive_days}} days plus the investigation window.
  • Access. Seller views filter by seller_id; carrier and fulfilment-centre breakdowns are internal.

Competing designs to accept. An event-sourced shipment aggregate with projections for the reconciled view. A single quantity ledger per shipment × SKU with typed movement rows (declared, received, found, reimbursed) instead of separate tables, if declared versions and box contents remain traceable. Matching unexpected units by a background job rather than at receiving.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Counters on the shipment row (lost under concurrent scans, double-counted on redelivery); declarations editable after shipping; boxes modelled only under their planned fulfilment centre; reimbursements not reversed when units are found; rates computed on shipments still receiving; unit-level events kept forever at {{daily_inbound_units}} units a day.

Incident guidance.

  • Pallets delivered to the wrong fulfilment centre: automated cases opened too early because "missing" was declared before the receiving window ended. Contain by pausing case creation for the affected shipments; match the boxes by label at the receiving fulfilment centre; transfer or re-point the shipments. Guardrail: cases open only after the receiving window ({{receive_days}} days) and a cross-centre label search.
  • Firmware redelivers a day of check-ins: the pipeline lacked event-id deduplication. Dedupe by event id (or scanner + sequence), rebuild the reconciled rows for affected shipments, correct sellable inventory with adjustments, and add a check that received ≤ declared + unexpected per shipment × SKU.
  • Reimbursed units later found: post a reimbursement reversal (or a seller-visible inventory adjustment) linked to the case; reconcile reimbursements against found units nightly; never delete the original reimbursement.

Follow-up guidance. (1) 100 = 96 sellable + 2 damaged + 1 found + 1 open (until resolved). (2) Reconcile against the version frozen at shipping; show earlier versions as history. (3) Box label is the join key; the box's physical location is an attribute of receiving events. (4) Cohort by shipped date; denominator declared units; final after the receiving window plus investigation. (5) Keep shipment × SKU and daily aggregates for years; unit events for months.

Rubric anchors. 2: one shipments table with received counters, no versioning, no discrepancy lifecycle. 3: declared / observed / resolved separation, versioned plans, append-only events, cases with resolutions and the invariant. 4: also wrong-centre matching by label, reimbursement reversal, receiving-window-aware rates and a retention plan for unit events.

Strong signals. States the invariant before tables; distinguishes received from sellable. Red flags. Overwriting counts; deleting a reimbursement; computing discrepancies the moment a box is late.

AMZ-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Runs. forecast_runs (run_id, model_version_id, forecast_date, inputs_snapshot_id, purpose production|challenger|debug, status created|complete|issued|superseded, issued_at, issued_by). A unique constraint on (forecast_date) WHERE status = 'issued' enforces one issued run per date; issuing is a separate, audited action, never a flag set by the job that produced the run.
  • Values. forecast_values (run_id, series_id, target_week, horizon_weeks, quantile, value), long form, append-only; partitioned by forecast_date (or run) and clustered by series. Horizon and quantile are keys, so adding P98 or extending the horizon adds rows, not columns.
  • Overrides. forecast_overrides (override_id, series_id, target_week, quantile NULL, value, author, reason, created_at, run_id); the decision forecast = override if present else issued value, exposed by a view.
  • Actuals. actuals (series_id, week, units, version, published_at) with corrections as new versions; availability (series_id, week, in_stock_share).
  • Accuracy. accuracy_results (eval_id, run_id, actuals_version, censor_policy, metric, slice keys: horizon, category, region, model_version, value, n_series). Median: volume-weighted absolute percentage error (Σ|F − A| ÷ Σ A) and bias (Σ(F − A) ÷ Σ A); quantiles: pinball (quantile) loss and coverage (share of actuals ≤ the quantile). Censored weeks (in-stock share below a threshold) are excluded or reported separately, or evaluated against an estimated demand; the policy is stored with the result.
  • Storage. {{series}} × {{horizon_weeks}} horizons × the quantile count, per week: hundreds of millions to tens of billions of rows a week at the top level. Keep full grain for the issued run for the decision-audit period (e.g. two years) in compressed columnar files; challengers at full grain for a few weeks, then only their accuracy results; debug runs expire quickly.

Competing designs to accept. One wide row per series and target week with quantile columns, if they show how schema changes are handled (a versioned schema per run). Storing forecasts as files per run with a catalog table, if issued runs are immutable and queryable. Evaluating against estimated (uncensored) demand from a separate model, if they mark it as an estimate.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Overwriting forecasts (decision audit impossible); "issued" set by any job; MAPE exploding on zero-sales weeks; censored weeks rewarding under-forecasts; accuracy computed against moving actuals without recording the version; storing every challenger and debug run at full grain.

Incident guidance.

  • Debug re-run marked issued: issuing was not a controlled action. Re-point the issued status to the original run (both runs still exist because values are immutable and keyed by run), notify planners whose purchase orders for the next {{horizon_weeks}} weeks read the wrong run, and re-evaluate those decisions. Guardrail: unique issued run per date, issuing only through an approval step, debug runs tagged and never eligible.
  • Accuracy improves during a stockout wave: censored weeks were scored against capped sales. Recompute with censored weeks excluded or flagged ({{stockout_share}} of series-weeks here) and publish both numbers; add the in-stock share to every accuracy slice.
  • Returns backfill flips a model comparison: the comparison did not pin the actuals version. Re-run against both versions, document the change, and revisit the promotion with the pinned, final actuals. Guardrail: accuracy results record actuals_version; comparisons for decisions use final actuals only.

Follow-up guidance. (1) series × horizons × quantiles per week; partition by forecast date, cluster by series; retention per run purpose. (2) Score both the model and the override separately; planners see the decision forecast, modellers see the model's accuracy. (3) Results with the old actuals version stay; new results labelled with the new version; reports say which. (4) Show the median error and coverage side by side by horizon; safety-stock decisions depend on the upper quantile. (5) Exclude or down-weight censored weeks, or compare against estimated demand, and state which.

Rubric anchors. 2: one forecast table overwritten each week, MAPE only, no notion of issued. 3: runs vs values, immutable issued runs, long-form values with horizon and quantile, versioned actuals, defined metrics. 4: also a censoring policy, reproducible evaluations with recorded actuals versions, overrides as records, and a storage and retention estimate.

Strong signals. Asks which forecast a decision used before designing storage; raises censoring unprompted. Red flags. Latest forecast wins; MAPE as the headline metric; deleting challenger results the moment a model is promoted.

AMZ-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Periods. settlement_periods (period_id, seller_id, marketplace, currency, start_at, end_at (UTC instants derived from the marketplace's local boundary), status open|closed|disbursement_sent|paid|failed, opening_balance_minor, closing_balance_minor, reserve_opening_minor, reserve_closing_minor). Closed periods are immutable.
  • Lines. settlement_lines (line_id, period_id, seller_id, currency, type principal|shipping|tax|commission|fulfilment_fee|refund_principal|refund_commission|refund_admin_fee|reimbursement|promotion|storage|reserve_hold|reserve_release|adjustment, amount_minor signed, source_type order|refund|reimbursement|fee_run|manual, source_id, order_id NULL, event_at, posted_at). Posting happens at shipment for orders; a correction is a new line in the open period referencing the line it corrects.
  • Reserve. A separate balance driven by reserve_hold and reserve_release lines with the rule version that produced them ({{reserve_rule}}); a rule change is a new rule version effective from a time, so the seller sees why the payout changed.
  • Disbursements. disbursements (disbursement_id, period_id, amount_minor, currency, sent_at, status sent|confirmed|failed, bank_reference, retry_of NULL). A period is paid only when the bank confirms; a failure posts a line returning the amount to the balance (or keeps the period in failed until retried).
  • Balance equation. closing = opening + Σ lines − Δ reserve − disbursed, per seller, marketplace and currency; negative closing carries forward.
  • Reconciliation. order_settlement_status (order_id, shipped_at, posted_period_id, posted_amount_minor, paid_at, refund_status, break_reason). Daily checks: Σ principal posted for shipments of day D = Σ order value shipped on D (by marketplace and currency); every disbursement amount = the period's computed payout; every refund line has a sale line (allowing for timing within a tolerance window).
  • Times. event_at (shipment or refund), posted_at, and period; the period boundary is defined once (UTC instants derived from the marketplace's local time) and printed on the statement.

Competing designs to accept. A full double-entry ledger per seller (accounts: available, reserve, payable to bank), as long as statements stay immutable and source keys are kept. Event-sourced settlement with statement projections. Daily (rather than period) balances with periods as views.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Matching by amount and date instead of keys; statements edited after close; reserve hidden inside line types; "paid" set on send instead of on confirmation; boundary time zones; currencies summed; refunds posted before sales at boundaries producing false breaks; recomputing every seller's history for each statement at {{monthly_transactions}} a month.

Incident guidance.

  • Rejected disbursements marked paid: status was set on send. Move the affected periods to failed, post lines returning the amounts to sellers' balances, notify sellers and retry with the corrected format. Guardrail: paid only on bank confirmation; reconcile disbursement outcomes daily against bank returns.
  • Fee applied twice: never edit the closed statements. Post a reversing adjustment line referencing the duplicate in the current period, explain it on the next statement, and add an idempotency key per (seller, fee run, period) on fee postings.
  • Refunds before sales at the boundary: timing, not loss. Reconcile by order id across periods with a tolerance window, mark "awaiting sale posting" instead of a break, and check that the boundary rule is applied the same way to both line types.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Equation with a worked period: prior-period sale's refund appears as negative lines now; failed disbursement adds the amount back. (2) Period boundary defined once and printed; the statement shows event time in local time and the period it posted to. (3) refund_principal, refund_commission (returned fee) and refund_admin_fee lines keyed by order_id and refund_id; net per order = Σ lines by order_id. (4) Join postings to shipments by order_id per day, marketplace and currency. (5) Reserve lines carry a rule version; the statement shows hold and release lines.

Rubric anchors. 2: a balance column updated in place, statements regenerated, matching by amount. 3: periods with typed signed lines, immutable closed statements, the balance equation, a reserve balance, source keys and a disbursement lifecycle. 4: also boundary time handling, reconciliation status per order with timing tolerance, idempotent fee postings and correct incident handling with compensating lines.

Strong signals. Separates event time from posting period; insists on keys over amount matching. Red flags. Editing closed statements; summing currencies; "paid" when the transfer is sent.

AMZ-L3-05.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL; {{as_of}} is the instance's as-of time)

WITH mv AS (                                   -- one row per event_id: the feed is at least once
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (event_id) event_id, fc_id, sku, kind, qty, reservation_id
  FROM inventory_movements
  WHERE occurred_at <= TIMESTAMPTZ '{{as_of}}'
  ORDER BY event_id, ingested_at
), stock AS (
  SELECT fc_id, sku, SUM(qty) AS on_hand
  FROM mv
  GROUP BY fc_id, sku
), shipped AS (
  SELECT reservation_id, -SUM(qty) AS units
  FROM mv
  WHERE kind = 'ship'
  GROUP BY reservation_id
), holds AS (
  SELECT r.fc_id, r.sku,
         SUM(CASE WHEN (r.cancelled_at IS NULL OR r.cancelled_at > TIMESTAMPTZ '{{as_of}}')
                   AND r.expires_at > TIMESTAMPTZ '{{as_of}}'
                  THEN GREATEST(r.qty - COALESCE(s.units, 0), 0)
                  ELSE 0 END) AS reserved
  FROM reservations r
  LEFT JOIN shipped s ON s.reservation_id = r.reservation_id
  WHERE r.reserved_at <= TIMESTAMPTZ '{{as_of}}'
  GROUP BY r.fc_id, r.sku
)
SELECT COALESCE(st.fc_id, h.fc_id) AS fc_id,
       COALESCE(st.sku, h.sku)     AS sku,
       COALESCE(st.on_hand, 0)     AS on_hand,
       COALESCE(h.reserved, 0)     AS reserved,
       GREATEST(COALESCE(st.on_hand, 0) - COALESCE(h.reserved, 0), 0) AS available_to_promise,
       GREATEST(COALESCE(h.reserved, 0) - COALESCE(st.on_hand, 0), 0) AS oversold_units
FROM stock st
FULL JOIN holds h ON h.fc_id = st.fc_id AND h.sku = st.sku
ORDER BY fc_id, sku;

Explanation. On hand and reserved live in different tables at different grains, so each is aggregated to (fc_id, sku) on its own and the two are combined with a FULL JOIN: a pair can have holds and no stock yet (the oversold rows) or stock and no holds. Shipping consumes a hold, so the units shipped per reservation (up to the as-of time) are subtracted from that reservation's qty before summing; otherwise a shipped unit is removed from on hand and still counted as reserved. Cancellation is inclusive (cancelled at or before the as-of time releases), expiry is exclusive (the hold lasts while as_of < expires_at). The deduplication by event_id costs nothing at Medium and Hard (event_id is unique there) and is required at Very Hard, where the feed redelivers events; occurred_at, not ingested_at, decides whether an event is in the books.

Complexity. One pass over movements up to the as-of time (a sort or hash for DISTINCT ON plus two hash aggregates) and one pass over reservations. In production, on hand per (fc, sku) comes from a materialised balance kept in step with the ledger, and only the tail since its watermark is read.

Dialect notes. DISTINCT ON is PostgreSQL; Snowflake, BigQuery and Spark SQL use QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY event_id ORDER BY ingested_at) = 1 (Spark without QUALIFY: a subquery on the row number); MySQL 8 uses the same row-number subquery. GREATEST exists in all of them, but in Snowflake and BigQuery it returns NULL if any argument is NULL, hence the COALESCE inside it. FULL JOIN is not supported in MySQL: union the keys of both sides and LEFT JOIN each. Timestamp literals: '…'::TIMESTAMP_TZ (Snowflake), TIMESTAMP '…' (BigQuery, UTC). None of these variants is executed here.

Edge cases built into the data. A receipt exactly at the as-of time (counts); a reservation made exactly at the as-of time (holds); a reservation cancelled exactly at the as-of time (releases); a reservation shipped after the as-of time (still holds at the as-of time, and its ship movement is not yet in on hand); a pair with holds and only a later receipt (on_hand 0, oversold); a pair with everything after the as-of time (no row). Hard adds a hold expiring exactly at the as-of time (lapsed), holds that expired earlier, signed cycle-count adjustments, and a reservation partly shipped before and partly after the as-of time. Very Hard adds redelivered events (same event_id, later ingested_at), including a redelivered ship, and a receipt that occurred before the as-of time but was ingested after it.

Common mistakes. Treating a boundary as exclusive; counting shipped units as still reserved; ignoring cancellations; starting from movements so hold-only pairs vanish; not flooring the outputs; (Hard+) ignoring expiry or treating expires_at = as_of as still held; (Very Hard) summing redelivered events twice, or filtering on ingested_at. Each has a diagnostic. Joining movements to reservations before aggregating multiplies rows and is a frequent cause of inflated totals.

Follow-up guidance. (1) A balance row per (fc, sku) updated in the same transaction as each ledger insert, or a snapshot at a watermark plus the tail; a nightly Σ ledger comparison proves it. (2) The storefront should use expiry-aware reads (lazy expiry) because the sweeper lags; this report uses the stated rule. (3) Running sum of holds per (fc, sku) ordered by reserved_at (window function), compared with on_hand: reservations whose running total exceeds on_hand are the unfillable ones. (4) At ingestion with a unique event_id is cheapest for every consumer; keeping the dedup in the query too is a cheap guard while the feed is at least once.

Rubric anchors. 2: right shape but shipped units counted as reserved, or hold-only pairs dropped. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains the sweeper gap, materialised balances with reconciliation, and the oversell allocation query.

Strong signals. Aggregates each side before joining without being told; asks what consumes a hold. Red flags. SELECT DISTINCT * as deduplication (rows differ in ingested_at); joining raw movements to raw reservations; filtering by ingested_at.
